title: Puerto Rico's Federal Fiscal Footprint, 1971–2025
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Puerto Rico's Federal Fiscal Footprint, 1971–2025
detail.abstract: Puerto Rico's GDP suggests a high-output economy, while GNP and personal income reveal a smaller resident-income base. This paper measures the other side of that external structure: federal fiscal flows through agency operations, external transfer receipts, and grants to government. Using Puerto Rico Planning Board Statistical Appendix tables, it reconstructs a federal-centered external fiscal footprint for FY1971–FY2025, including historical agency-expenditure and receipt observations transcribed from scanned editions. The footprint was already large by the mid-1970s, at 17.0% of GNP in 1971 and 37.2% in 1976. It remained near one-quarter to one-third of GNP through much of the 1990s and early 2000s, then rose from 25.3% in 2005 to 66.4% in 2025, after peaking at 76.6% in 2022. The post-2005 rise was mainly driven by flow growth: external flows grew 318.5%, while GNP grew 59.6%. The measure is gross and federal-centered rather than net or perfectly federal-only, but it provides a consistent baseline for evaluating Puerto Rico's fiscal integration and economic exposure.

title: The Silent Struggle: Legal Support for Child Domestic Workers in India
affiliations: O.P. Jindal University and O.P. Jindal University

detail.title: The Silent Struggle: Legal Support for Child Domestic Workers in India
detail.abstract: Domestic Violence is an overriding issue in the world. It could be on anyone irrespective of caste, gender, race, or age but the biggest victims have been women and children. According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), domestic labour is the most common occupation for females under the age of 16. Millions of children serve as domestic servants around the world, yet they are typically neglected, disregarded, and are not safeguarded by labour laws, putting them especially at increased risk of terrible human rights violations. This study intends to evaluate the effectiveness of national laws in preventing this contemporary form of slavery and protecting child domestic workers. It also looks at how stronger regulations can make it easier to put preventative measures into place. While there are several international rules intended to protect juvenile domestic workers, many national laws ignore this issue. Despite not having any legal force in India, the conventions and recommendations of the ILO have had a significant impact on the development of the country's labour laws. India, being a populist country and developing country faces the issues of child domestic labour too but the government has not been completely ignorant of this fact. The government has made a comprehensive policy and legal framework which gives a guarantee to the youth that they are protected. In Francis Coralie Mullin vs. Union Territory of Delhi, the court applied Article 21 to clarify that the protection of children from abuse is an integral part of the Indian Constitution too. They deserve all the right to be raised in a healthy environment and have freedom like every citizen. Along with framing national laws on it, India has ratified the international treaties on child labour which brings half a billion Indian children up to 18 years under its protection. As per ILO, the work constituted under child labour would entail all mentally, physically, morally, and socially dangerous activities for children or which interfere with their ability to attend school. In India, there has been no centralized system to keep track of several child labourers in domestic work. Due to the difficulties in getting access to the private spaces where these kids work, little research has been done on the subject. This study examines India's current legal and judicial system and concludes that while international agreements provide some protection, there is room for improvement through vigilant oversight, effective enforcement, and strong advocacy. The elimination of ingrained social and cultural norms that support child domestic work depends on these measures. The article also provides practical implementation techniques and steps to end this disguised slavery in India while analyzing and making you aware of the existing laws and judgements of the Indian Courts. There is a necessity for robust social security laws that are specially designed for child domestic workers to end the cycle of exploitation and protect these defenseless youth.

detail.abstract:
This policy brief builds on the SSRN working paper Beyond Dependence: External Structural Coherence and Geoeconomic Vulnerability: Evidence from Portugal, Canada, and Australia (2019–2024) and incorporates preliminary extensions of the ESC dataset to additional European economies.

The brief introduces External Structural Coherence (ESC) as a diagnostic framework for assessing the alignment between the geographical distribution of inward FDI and merchandise trade flows across geoeconomic blocs. It argues that the EU’s current economic security instruments measure concentration but not coherence, leaving a structural gap in the assessment of external vulnerability.

Applied to Portugal, Canada, and Australia, the ESC framework identifies three structurally distinct configurations: regional coherence, concentrated coherence, and structural incoherence. Preliminary evidence from additional European economies suggests that structural coherence is relatively high across EU Member States but varies sufficiently to warrant systematic monitoring rather than assumption.

The brief proposes three policy implications: complementing existing concentration-based monitoring with coherence assessment, accounting for heterogeneity across Member States, and recognising that restructuring external dependencies operates on decade-long time horizons. More broadly, it argues that economic security depends not only on understanding the scale of external dependencies, but also on assessing whether different forms of dependence point in the same geoeconomic direction.

title: To be or not to be by-object
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Faculty of Law

detail.title: To be or not to be by-object

detail.abstract: Few distinctions in EU competition law are as indeterminate - yet as consequential - as the one made between restrictions by object and those by effect. For all practical purposes, arrangements falling within the former category constitute an infringement of Article 101, with only limited scope for justification or exemption. In light of this, it is striking that the distinction - although derived directly from the wording of Article 101 and unchanged since its inception - remains unsettled. This paper seeks to renew the effort to articulate practical principles for identifying by-object restrictions. It proposes a focus on an arrangement’s capacity to realize a formulated theory of harm of an aggravated nature, in circumstances where no plausible alternative, legitimate justifications are apparent: an assessment to be implemented in steps.

title: Optimal Taxation in the Automation Era
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Optimal Taxation in the Automation Era
detail.abstract: This paper studies the optimal tax-and-transfer policy when automation raises productivity but displaces unskilled workers. Using a general equilibrium model calibrated to the U.S. economy, we compute the steady-state social welfare-maximizing rate of each of four tax instruments: capital income taxation, unskilled wage taxation, taxation on automation capital (i.e., a robot tax), and consumption taxation. Following an increase in the productivity of automation-related capital, the welfare-maximizing capital income tax rate is small, and the welfare-maximizing robot tax rate is zero at the baseline labor-automation elasticity because their long-run investment distortions largely offset their redistributive social benefits. In the baseline simulation, aggregate welfare is maximized by lowering the unskilled wage tax rate and/or raising the consumption and capital income tax rates, whilst the social welfare improvement is always the largest for optimal consumption taxation. When unskilled labor and automation-related capital are highly substitutable, the optimal consumption tax rate increases, and the additional government revenue is redistributed to displaced unskilled workers.

detail.title: Digitalization and Credit Markets: Evidence from E-Invoicing

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de España Working Paper No. 2619

detail.abstract: We document the effects of electronic invoicing (eInvoicing) on credit markets. By making invoices more standardized, verifiable, and harder to falsify, eInvoicing changes lenders’ information sets, facilitating invoice-based financing and credit risk assessment. We exploit a regional eInvoicing mandate and administrative credit data using a difference-in-differences design to provide three main insights. First, credit reallocates toward firms already relying on invoice-based credit (“invoice firms”) and away from non-invoice firms. Second, the cost of (non-)invoice credit falls (rises) for (non-)invoice firms, consistent with a supply-driven mechanism. Third, banks' information production changes: eInvoicing widens (reduces) the dispersion of rates and banks' risk assessments and improves (worsens) their predictive accuracy for (non-)invoice firms. Overall, eInvoicing reshapes credit market outcomes, with uneven effects across borrowers.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether edge-preserving filters improve real-time extraction of macro-financial regime information in an implementable U.S. sector-allocation strategy. The state vector comprises four public market-based indicators: the VIX, the Russell 2000-to-S&P 500 ratio, the consumer discretionary-to-staples ratio, and the nancials-to-utilities ratio. The investable universe consists of the nine Select Sector SPDR ETFs. Six real-time signal-extraction methods are compared: the raw panel, Savitzky-Golay, Perona-Malik anisotropic diffusion, a recursively estimated Hodrick-Prescott trend, endpoint LOESS, and a local-level Kalman filter. The ltered indicators are standardized with trailing 48-month z-scores, aggregated into a composite macro score, classied into expansion, slowdown, and stress regimes using expanding quantile thresholds, and mapped into a monthly long-only allocation to the sector with the highest trailing 60-month regime-conditional mean return. Over the common out-of-sample period from February 2004 through July 2026, the raw strategy delivers a 5.60% annualized return with a Sharpe ratio of 0.304. Savitzky-Golay raises those gures to 13.78% and 0.707, while Perona-Malik delivers 15.85% and 0.820, outperforming the other real-time smoothers. Relative to the raw timing rule, Perona-Malik yields a 9.50 percentage-point annualized mean return spread with a paired t-statistic of 3.38 and positive moving-block and stationary-bootstrap condence intervals. Relative to the equal-weight sector benchmark, the gain is economically positive but less decisive under conventional two-sided tests. The results therefore support a strong claim that edge-preserving ltering improves the information content of the raw regime signal and a more qualied claim relative to passive sector exposure. Multiple-testing diagnostics based on White's Reality Check, Hansen's Superior Predictive Ability test, the Deated Sharpe Ratio, and the Probability of Backtest Overtting reinforce that interpretation.

title: The Price of Lower Price Caps: How Pharmaceutical Price Caps Affect the Supplier Landscape and Shortages

detail.title: The Price of Lower Price Caps: How Pharmaceutical Price Caps Affect the Supplier Landscape and Shortages

detail.abstract: The Dutch Medicines Pricing Act (Wet geneesmiddelenprijzen, WGP) establishes price caps for medicines to control pharmaceutical expenditures. While the WGP has contributed to lower medicine costs, concerns have emerged that reduced prices may undermine supplier participation and increase medicine shortages. This study examines the relationship between price cap reductions, supplier dynamics, and medicine shortages using comprehensive longitudinal data on prescription clusters (PRKs) in the Netherlands. We find that, over the past decade, price caps have declined, the number of suppliers per PRK has decreased, market concentration has increased, and shortage exposure has risen. Exploiting substantial price cap reductions (≥10%) and comparing affected PRKs with matched control clusters, we show that price cap decreases increase the market share in shortage by 1.34 percentage points on average, equivalent to approximately 4.9 additional shortage days per PRK per year. At the same time, price cap reductions are associated with declines in the number of suppliers and active suppliers by 1.81% and 3.00%, respectively. These effects are particularly pronounced among low-priced, low-revenue, multi-source, and price-constrained medicines. Additional analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity across market conditions, with the strongest effects observed among medicines with limited economic margins and weaker supplier incentives. The findings remain robust across alternative identification strategies, shortage definitions, time windows, and smaller price cap shocks. Overall, our results highlight an important trade-off between pharmaceutical cost containment and supply resilience, suggesting that pricing policies should consider their potential effects on supplier participation and medicine availability.

title: The Workforce Consequences of Ending Mandatory Union Fees: Evidence from Janus v. AFSCME

detail.title: The Workforce Consequences of Ending Mandatory Union Fees: Evidence from Janus v. AFSCME

detail.abstract: Public-sector unions shape how state and local governments staff and size their workforces, yet clean shocks to union power are rare. The 2018 ruling by the U.S. Supreme Court in Janus v. AFSCME provided one, eliminating mandatory agency fees in the 21 states that had previously permitted them. I use a difference-in-differences design comparing affected states with right-to-work states and draw on two complementary datasets: three waves of the Census of Governments (CoG) and a balanced 2011-2025 annual panel that combines the CoG with the Annual Survey of Public Employment and Payroll. I find that Janus reduced part-time employment by 6.2 to 8.4 percent while leaving full-time employment unchanged, thereby raising the full-time share of the workforce by 1.13 to 1.75 percentage points. A simple model rationalizes this pattern: because union power sustained the part-time periphery, weakening it shifts the adjustment onto the least-protected positions rather than the full-time core. Per-worker earnings are unchanged for full-time and part-time workers alike, in both datasets. I additionally confirm the earnings null using individual-level CPS and state-level QCEW data.

title: Dynamic Causal Portfolio Choice: Hedging the Rotation of the Common-Driver Manifold
affiliations: University of Reading

detail.title: Dynamic Causal Portfolio Choice: Hedging the Rotation of the Common-Driver Manifold
detail.abstract: When a portfolio is conditioned on a minimal set of observable drivers under which its assets become mutually independent over the investment horizon, the dynamic investment problem acquires a distinctive geometric structure. We study continuous-time portfolio choice in this setting. The conditioning representation, rather than the asset vector, becomes the natural state of the problem, and it moves: the sensitivity of returns to the drivers depends on the state, the conditioning set may itself change over time, and the induced information geometry both rotates and, at discrete instants, jumps. The optimal policy separates into a static component that allocates along the conditioning geometry at each instant and an intertemporal component that hedges the predictable motion of that geometry, a first-order effect in the model rather than a refinement, placing the coordinates of the information geometry in the role played by exogenous state variables in classical intertemporal asset pricing. Because the problem is organized by the drivers, its computational cost is governed by their number rather than by the number of assets. Changes in the conditioning set generate a risk that continuous trading cannot span, so the market is incomplete in the direction of its own geometry. The analysis is carried out in a controlled diffusion model, and the resulting structure is illustrated on synthetic economies designed to isolate each mechanism.

title: Motorcyclist Behaviour in Car-Following Conditions: Effects of an Auditory ARAS in an Immersive Virtual Reality Simulator
affiliations: Roma Tre University, , Roma Tre University and Roma Tre University

detail.title: Motorcyclist Behaviour in Car-Following Conditions: Effects of an Auditory ARAS in an Immersive Virtual Reality Simulator
detail.abstract: Motorcyclists represent one of the most vulnerable categories of road users, with a high exposure to risk in dynamic traffic environments, particularly in car-following conditions, when the ability to correctly perceive distance, anticipate the behaviour of leading vehicles, and maintain appropriate safety margins is crucial. This study investigates motorcyclist behaviour in car-following conditions through an immersive virtual reality (VR) simulator, with particular focus on the effects of an auditory-based Advanced Rider Assistance System (ARAS) designed to support longitudinal control of the rider. The experimental setup integrates a fixed-base Honda® Riding Trainer (HRT) as a physical user interface with a Meta® Quest 3S Head-Mounted Display (HMD), providing a fully immersive visual environment. The simulation scenario was developed using a Building Information Modelling (BIM) workflow and implemented in Unity®, ensuring a high level of ecological validity while maintaining control over experimental variables. The study considers three interaction conditions of the rider with a lead vehicle (LV): constant speed (CS) of the LV, gradual deceleration (GD, -3.0 m/s²) of the LV, and emergency deceleration (ED, -6.0 m/s²) of the LV, each reproduced both with and without ARAS support for the rider. A total of 48 participants were included in the final analysis following a data screening procedure. Motorcyclist behaviour was evaluated through objective kinematic indicators, including relative distance, Time Headway (TH), and time-based risk exposure, as well as through subjective assessments collected via post-test questionnaires. A Generalized Linear Model (GLM) was applied for the analysis of the behavioural and kinematic variables. In addition, for the time-based risk indicators, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was adopted due to the presence of non-normal and zero-inflated distributions. The results consistently demonstrate that the ARAS significantly improves motorcyclist behaviour across all tested interaction conditions. In the CS condition, the system leads to increased relative distances and higher TH values, along with a substantial reduction in the rider's time spent in high-risk conditions. In both GD and ED conditions, the ARAS encourages earlier and more controlled responses, which leads to lower deceleration rates and almost no exposure to critical risk. Under emergency conditions, the system effectively reduces the rider’s time spent in the most critical safety zone to zero. Subjective evaluations align with objective findings, confirming high immersion, realism, and user engagement, thus supporting the validity of the VR environment. The ARAS was positively rated for usefulness and clarity, with auditory feedback effectively avoiding additional visual load and achieving high user acceptance. Cybersickness was generally low, and HMD constraints did not significantly affect performance, indicating a satisfactory balance between immersion and usability. Overall, the integration of an auditory ARAS within an immersive VR simulation framework demonstrates significant potential in enhancing motorcyclist safety. The results highlight the effectiveness of audio warnings in supporting anticipatory behaviour and reducing exposure to critical risk conditions. These findings contribute to the development of rider-centred assistance systems and provide valuable insights for future applications in road safety and road user behaviour s

title: Semantic-Topological Antifragility: A Quantitative RAG Expert System for Continuous-Time SDE Volatility Forecasting
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Ferdowsi University of Mashhad (FUM)

detail.title: Semantic-Topological Antifragility: A Quantitative RAG Expert System for Continuous-Time SDE Volatility Forecasting
detail.abstract: The accurate calibration of continuous-time Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) is critical for financial expert systems. However, classical autoregressive models rely on local stationarity, resulting in a severe, reactive phase lag during structural market crashes. Conversely, continuous-time deep learning models (Neural SDEs) often generate mathematically explosive parameters known as epistemic hallucination when processing out-of-distribution events. To resolve this critical methodological disparity, we propose Semantic-Topological Antifragility (STA), a Quantitative Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Q-RAG) system engineered for robust stochastic parameter synthesis. The STA framework fuses topological price geometry (measured via Jensen-Shannon Divergence) with semantic market narratives (encoded via FinBERT). The Q-RAG engine queries a historical vector database to retrieve contextually analogous priors. These priors are dynamically integrated with an econometric baseline through a novel Bimodal Elastic Contrastive Gate. We mathematically prove that this gating architecture ensures uniform Lipschitz continuity, thereby guaranteeing the existence of a unique, non-explosive SDE solution. Extensive evaluations on S\&P 500 data (2008-2024) confirm that the STA framework eliminates the autoregressive phase lag and significantly reduces the asymmetric QLIKE loss to 0.070. Furthermore, when deployed in a volatility-targeting portfolio, the system exhibits genuine antifragility, successfully converting systemic disorder into protective crisis alpha.
